Problem 11. Following water from North Fork
River systems form directed networks: water has a direction, tributaries join larger streams, and upstream/downstream are relational concepts.
North Fork flows into Meadow River; Red Brook flows into Meadow River; Meadow River flows into Blue Creek.
If river X flows into river Y, X is upstream of Y. Upstream relations can be followed through several confluences. Downstream is the reverse direction of flow.
Is North Fork upstream of Blue Creek? Can water from North Fork reach Blue Creek through the stated network?

1. Rewrite the facts as arrows: North Fork→Meadow River, Red Brook→Meadow River, Meadow River→Blue Creek. 2. Follow arrows starting from North Fork. 3. An arrow path reaches Blue Creek, so North Fork is upstream of Blue Creek.
Yes; water from North Fork can reach Blue Creek.
A river network can be reasoned about like any directed network; following the arrows is more reliable than guessing from names.
Directed graph; edge X→Y means water can flow from X to Y; query reachability.

Problem 16. Crossing the fictional border network of Birch
Political maps can be treated as adjacency networks. This lets us reason about border crossings without relying on memorized real-world geography.

Countries are represented by the fictional states Birch, Cedar, Northfield, Pine, Alder, Willow. Shared borders: Birch–Cedar, Cedar–Northfield, Northfield–Pine, Birch–Alder, Alder–Willow, Willow–Pine.
Crossing one border corresponds to traversing one graph edge. A route may use only listed borders. A state is unavoidable only if every feasible route passes through it.
What is the fewest number of border crossings needed to travel from Birch to Pine? Is Cedar necessarily crossed?
